title: Lockheed's ARRW Goes Into Production as Europe's Missile-Repair and Drone-Defence Map Redraws Itself
subhead: The US Air Force moves a once-cancelled hypersonic weapon into serial production, Poland wins a European PAC-3 maintenance hub, and three European counter-drone designs land in the same week — the industrial geography of air and missile defence is being rebuilt closer to the front.

sections.heading: ARRW Moves From Test Article to Production Line
sections.body:
The US Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract in late September to put the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) into production and fielding, the service announced on Monday according to Defense News. The missile is a solid-rocket-boosted boost-glide design that accelerates past Mach 5 before releasing a hypersonic glide vehicle, meant to strike heavily defended, time-sensitive targets from standoff range.

Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink called it 'a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,' and Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach framed ARRW as giving the Joint Force a rapid response option in highly contested environments. The contract ran through the Pentagon's Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract.

What makes the award notable is the program's history. The Air Force moved to halt ARRW purchases in 2023 after failed tests, pivoting to the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile. In 2025, then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allen told Congress the service intended to revive it with new money in the fiscal 2026 budget. Three years from cancellation to production is a fast reversal by hypersonics standards, and the service declined to say how many missiles or on what timeline, citing operational security.
sections.whyItMatters: A program cancelled for test failures has been rehabilitated and funded. The US now has a second boost-glide line moving alongside HACM, which spreads risk — but the refusal to disclose quantity suggests low-rate initial output rather than a deep magazine.

sections.heading: Poland Gets the European PAC-3 Repair Hub — Germany, Netherlands and Sweden Get the Supply Chain
sections.body:
Washington selected Poland to host a new European maintenance facility for PAC-3 interceptors, Defense News reported from Warsaw. Pentagon acquisition chief Michael Duffey said the hub would put 'partnership into action' on NATO's eastern front, while supply-chain integration is to be led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed Poland competed hard for the facility, beating 'several ambitious competitors.' Poland signed a roughly $4.75 billion deal in 2018 for two Configuration 3+ Patriot batteries, launched a second phase in 2022 for six more, and announced in December 2025 that the first two batteries reached full operational readiness.

The hub sits inside a wider push: European allies are negotiating with Washington over licensed PAC-3 MSE production in Europe, with Poland, Ukraine and Germany among those lobbying for domestic manufacture. Germany and the US have separately signed an agreement making Germany an additional production hub for scarce American equipment.

Lockheed Martin also said separately that Raytheon's overseas business now accounts for 37% of its $130 billion backlog (52% excluding the quarter's Tomahawk and AMRAAM multiyear conversions), with CEO Chris Calio citing Germany, Poland and Japan as the 2027 spenders to watch, per Defence Industry Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: Maintenance is the bottleneck that turns an interceptor order into a usable stockpile. Putting turnaround on the eastern flank cuts transit time for Patriot rounds in the theatre most likely to burn through them — and gives Poland an industrial foothold it can trade on later.

sections.heading: Europe's Counter-Drone Sector Answers the Cheap-Interceptor Problem Three Different Ways
sections.body:
Three European firms put counter-drone hardware on the table in the same news cycle, and each is attacking a different part of the cost curve.

Germany's Helsing unveiled Contra, an AI-controlled air defence system built on its Altra command-and-control platform, paired with two container-launched interceptors: AD-1 Inferno, jet-powered and designed to loiter and make repeated engagement attempts, and AD-2 Ambush, solid-rocket propelled at Mach 2.5 with range beyond 20 km. Co-founder Niklas Köhler framed it as ending 'the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets.' Helsing says the interceptors will be built at its Resilience Factories but did not disclose unit prices.

Czech firm KBP International showed GRYF at the Future Forces Forum in Prague — a piston-engined carrier drone with 12 hours of endurance, a 500 km range, and four hardpoints for roughly 5 kg interceptors or small interceptor drones. The airframe is not the weapon; it loiters and releases effectors. Defense News separately reported Helsing's interceptors as aimed at Russia's jet-powered Geran drones, and that Estonia is weighing light jet aircraft to shoot down the same class of target.

France tested a counter-drone laser aboard the Charles de Gaulle at sea, per Defence Industry Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: Everyone has converged on the same insight — a Shahed-class drone cannot be answered with a million-dollar missile — but the solutions diverge: AI-coordinated interceptor swarms, airborne carriers, and directed energy. The winner will be whoever gets unit cost low enough to be spent at scale, and none of the three has published a price.

sections.heading: Airbus and BAE Open Talks on GCAP as Germany Weighs Its Fighter Future
sections.body:
Airbus and BAE Systems are expected to discuss cooperation around the Global Combat Air Programme, according to Financial Times reporting on October 25 followed by Reuters on October 26, as cited by Global Defense Corp. The talks would reportedly span GCAP itself, collaborative combat aircraft, and the digital 'combat cloud' linking aircraft, sensors and drones.

The caveats are substantial. No decisions are expected; BAE called the meeting 'routine'; Reuters said it could not independently verify the meeting. Airbus stated it is open to partnerships provided German, Spanish and wider European industry get 'substantial and equal participation' in development, production and operational use. Airbus Defence and Space chief Michael Schöllhorn has said the company would expect a meaningful industrial role.

GCAP is already institutionalised: the UK, Italy and Japan run it through the GCAP International Government Organisation, with Edgewing (BAE, Leonardo, Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement Co.) responsible for design. A £4.6 billion contract with Edgewing was finalised in July 2026 and Britain has committed £8.6 billion over four years, targeting service entry from 2035.
sections.whyItMatters: This lands weeks after the FCAS collapse pushed France to go it alone on its next-generation fighter. If Germany leans toward GCAP, Europe's two future-fighter tracks consolidate into one — but the programme's equal-partnership structure makes adding a fourth government an industrial negotiation, not an announcement.

sections.heading: India Becomes Europe's Ammunition Supplier
sections.body:
Indian defence exports to Europe have surged on ammunition and artillery demand, Defense News reported from New Delhi. Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said on October 23 that the EU's ReArm Europe initiative combined with India's expanding manufacturing base is driving the growth.

The numbers: India exported at least $872 million of ammunition in the four years since Russia's invasion of Ukraine — a more than 1,600% increase over the preceding four-year period, per a Bloomberg report citing Trade Data Monitor data. Romania, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Croatia and Poland were among the largest buyers; the goods include artillery shells, small-calibre ammunition, mortars, propellants and explosives. European destinations accounted for 40% of India's total arms and ammunition exports in the last financial year, according to Samuel Rajiv of the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses.

Separately, the Pentagon and BAE signed a deal in October for up to 25,000 precision-guided munition kits per year, and the US Army is seeking manufacturers for 155mm howitzer barrels amid rising demand — the same bottleneck seen from the other side of the supply chain.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's shell shortage was solved partly by outsourcing to a non-European, non-NATO supplier that Russia still courts. That is a dependency Europe will have to price in — and a genuine industrial opening for India's private and state ammunition makers.

sections.heading: Britain Stays Out of the Canada-Led Defence Bank
sections.body:
Britain will not join the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, Defense News reported, citing a person familiar with the matter — a setback to creating the world's first global defence bank. Germany had previously declined and remains an observer in charter negotiations, per its finance ministry.

The two governments said on Sunday they would instead build a framework linking Britain's Multilateral Defence Mechanism with the DSRB as two complementary institutions. Per sources cited by Defense News, they could not agree on the joint institution's headquarters location, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, or rules for new members. The MDM is to focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement financing and aggregating NATO demand to cut costs; the DSRB, based in Canada, is to focus on sovereign lending to defence industries and supply chains.
sections.whyItMatters: The financing layer of European rearmament is fragmenting at the exact moment capital demand is peaking. Two parallel institutions with overlapping mandates and unresolved membership rules will slow the pace at which money reaches production lines.

sections.heading: US Navy Opens Its Frigate Market to Foreign Designs
sections.body:
Babcock confirmed to The Telegraph on October 25 that it will offer its Arrowhead 140 — the basis of the Royal Navy's Type 31 — for a US Navy surface combatant requirement, after Trump's August 13, 2026 memorandum permitted limited foreign warship construction, Global Defense Corp reported. Babcock has held preliminary Pentagon meetings and could partner with Huntington Ingalls Industries to build in US yards. An expression of interest was expected by end-October; no formal bid exists.

The competition is crowded: Japan's Mogami-class, South Korea's Chungnam-class and Turkey's Istanbul-class are all in the frame. The Type 31 has not entered operational service and its baseline lacks shipborne sonar for sustained ASW — a notable gap given a UK parliamentary committee found the Royal Navy has a 'serious' anti-submarine warfare shortfall. The memo allows foreign yards only for the first two hulls, with later ships built in the US; the Secretary of War must submit a surface-combatant acquisition plan by November 12, 2026.

Elsewhere in naval industry: Navantia launched the Spanish Navy's second F110 frigate four months ahead of schedule and a seventh corvette for Saudi Arabia, and Hanwha Defense USA is taking a controlling stake in Philly Shipyard for planned US Navy work.
sections.whyItMatters: The Constellation-class cutback left a gap the US cannot fill domestically at speed, so the market is opening to allied designs. Whoever wins sets the template for licensed foreign warship production in America — a precedent far larger than one frigate order.

bottomLine: The through-line today is production geography. A hypersonic missile long written off is back in serial production at Lockheed; PAC-3 maintenance is moving to Poland while its supply chain stays in Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden; and Europe's counter-drone startups are competing on cost per intercept rather than performance per shot. Europe's ammunition and financing layers are being built outside the continent — Indian factories and a Canadian bank Britain refuses to join. The bottleneck across every one of these stories is the same: not design, but how fast industry can deliver and sustain what has already been ordered.
sources: Defense News, Defence Industry Europe, Global Defense Corp, Reuters, Financial Times, The Telegraph, Bloomberg / Trade Data Monitor, Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, Royal United Services Institute-adjacent UK parliamentary committee findings (via Defense News)
